Survival-Supervised Bayesian Matrix Factorization for Prognostic Molecular Programs in Pancreatic Cancer

Author

Andrew J. Walther

Published

October 14, 2026

Summary

We describe two Bayesian matrix factorization models that link molecular programs to overall survival in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Both factor molecular data into nonnegative patient activities and feature loadings and enter survival through a Cox model on the projection of each patient’s data onto the loadings, a score that can be computed for new patients. The single-modality model, trained on 273 patients from two cohorts measured on different platforms, has a mean concordance of 0.627 across five held-out cohorts (616 patients) and a small advantage over an independently tuned two-step factorization-then-Cox comparator. In the evaluated configuration survival shapes the coefficients but not the loadings. Its four retained programs correspond to the basal-like and classical tumor axes and to stromal and immune components. The multimodal model shares activities across matched expression and methylation and removes factors by an approximate evidence criterion. It recovers the true rank in simulation at lower noise, but on real data it removes no factor, most fits do not converge, and adding methylation does not demonstrably improve prediction.

1 Methods

1.1 Notation

Patients are indexed by \(i = 1, \dots, n\), molecular features by \(j\), factors (programs) by \(k = 1, \dots, K\), and data blocks (modalities) by \(m\). Patient \(i\) has observed time \(t_i\) and event indicator \(\delta_i\) (1 for death, 0 for censoring). The single-modality data are an \(n \times p\) matrix \(Y\); the multimodal data are matched blocks \(Y_m\) of dimension \(n \times p_m\), here gene expression (\(m = \mathrm{expr}\)) and DNA methylation (\(m = \mathrm{meth}\)). The symbol \(\beta\) is reserved for survival coefficients; methylation measurements are written \(Y_{\mathrm{meth}}\). For any random quantity \(\theta\) under the variational posterior \(q\), \(\bar\theta = E_q\theta\) and \(\overline{\theta^2} = E_q\theta^2\).

Three patient-level quantities are kept apart. The latent activities \(L \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{n \times K}\) are posterior scores in the reconstruction \(Y \approx LF^\top\) and exist only for training patients. The projection scores are the product of a patient’s data with the posterior-mean loadings; they enter the Cox predictor and can be computed for new patients. The signature scores, used only in biological characterization, are means of within-cohort standardized expression over a selected gene set.

1.2 Single-modality model

Reconstruction and priors. The training matrix is modeled as \[ y_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^K L_{ik} F_{jk} + e_{ij}, \qquad e_{ij} \sim N(0, \tau_j^{-1}), \tag{1}\] with independent point-exponential priors \(L_{ik} \sim g_{L,k}\) and \(F_{jk} \sim g_{F,k}\) (a point mass at zero mixed with an exponential distribution) whose parameters are estimated by empirical Bayes within each factor, using the R package ebnm. Each feature has its own residual precision \(\tau_j\), estimated by maximum likelihood.

Survival predictor. Survival follows a Cox model whose linear predictor is the projection of the patient’s data onto unit-length loading directions, \[ \eta_i = \sum_{k=1}^K \tilde Z_{ik}\tilde\beta_k, \qquad \tilde Z = Y \bar F D^{-1}, \quad D = \mathrm{diag}(d_1, \dots, d_K), \tag{2}\] with \(\tilde\beta_k \sim N(0, \sigma_k^2)\) and \(\sigma_k^2\) estimated per factor. In the joint target that motivates the method, the loadings are random and \(d_k = \lVert F_{\cdot k}\rVert_2\) is a function of them (Appendix A). The evaluated algorithm instead fixes, at the start of each sweep \(r\), the norms \(d_k^{(r)} = \lVert \bar F^{(r-1)}_{\cdot k}\rVert_2\) of the current posterior-mean loadings and the projection \(\tilde Z^{(r)} = Y\bar F^{(r-1)}[D^{(r)}]^{-1}\), and treats both as known covariates for the rest of the sweep. The saved fit stores the norms \(D_*\) formed at the start of its final sweep, and every prediction uses \(D_*\) with the final \(\bar F\). Normalization removes the arbitrary Euclidean magnitude of each loading column, which the reconstruction does not determine: \(L_{\cdot k}F_{\cdot k}^\top\) is unchanged when \(L_{\cdot k}\) is multiplied and \(F_{\cdot k}\) divided by the same constant. The coefficients are therefore per unit of normalized projection, not per standard deviation. A column of \(\bar F\) that is identically zero gives a zero projection.

Cox working approximation. Let \(\hat\eta\) be the predictor at the start of a sweep and \(a_i = \exp(\hat\eta_i)\hat H_0(t_i)\), where \(\hat H_0\) is the Breslow cumulative baseline hazard; \(a_i\) is the expected number of events for patient \(i\) under \(\hat\eta\). We retain the Breslow score \(u_i = \delta_i - a_i\) and replace the exact negative Hessian of the log partial likelihood, which couples patients through shared risk sets, by the diagonal working curvature \(w_i = \max(a_i, 10^{-6})\). Completing the square in the resulting quadratic gives \[ \log \mathrm{PL}(\eta) \approx \mathrm{const} - \tfrac12 \sum_i w_i (z_i - \eta_i)^2, \qquad z_i = \hat\eta_i + u_i / w_i. \tag{3}\] This is a Poisson-style working approximation, not the second-order Taylor expansion of the partial likelihood: the exact diagonal of the negative Hessian is smaller than \(a_i\) (Appendix A.2).

Where survival enters. The survival weight \(\alpha \in (0,1]\) multiplies the working term in the coefficient update. The evaluated value \(\alpha = 0.5\) leaves each coefficient’s pseudo-observation unchanged and halves its precision. The loading weight \(\alpha_F\) mixes a reconstruction contribution (weight \(1 - \alpha_F\)) and a survival contribution (weight \(\alpha_F\)) in the update of \(F\); the evaluated configuration uses \(\alpha_F = 0\). The activities \(L\) do not appear in \(\eta\). Survival therefore does not enter the updates of \(L\) or \(F\) in the evaluated fits: it determines \(\tilde\beta\), and through the stopping rule it can affect which iterate is returned, so the fitted loadings need not equal those of a separately converged unsupervised factorization. The coefficient update treats \(\tilde Z\) as fixed and does not propagate posterior uncertainty in \(F\).

Algorithm 1. Single-modality fit and prediction.

Inputs: training matrix \(Y\) standardized within cohort; times and event indicators \((t_i, \delta_i)\); starting rank \(K\); weights \(\alpha\), \(\alpha_F\); tolerance \(\epsilon\); iteration cap \(T\).

  1. Initialize \(\bar L\) and \(\bar F\) from the absolute values of the leading \(K\) left and right singular vectors of \(Y\), each scaled by the square root of its singular value. Set \(\bar{\tilde\beta} = 0\) and \(\tau_j = 1/\widehat{\mathrm{var}}(y_{\cdot j})\).
  2. For sweeps \(r = 1, \dots, T\):
    1. Form \(D^{(r)}\) and \(\tilde Z^{(r)} = Y\bar F D^{-1}\), the predictor \(\hat\eta = \tilde Z\bar{\tilde\beta}\), and the working quantities \((w, z)\) of Equation 3. Hold these fixed for the rest of the sweep.
    2. For \(k = 1, \dots, K\):
      1. update \(q(\tilde\beta_k)\) by empirical-Bayes normal means with pseudo-observation \(x = B/A\) and standard error \(A^{-1/2}\), where \(A = \alpha\sum_i w_i\tilde Z_{ik}^2\) and \(B = \alpha\sum_i w_i\tilde Z_{ik}(z_i - \sum_{l \ne k}\tilde Z_{il}\bar{\tilde\beta}_l)\);
      2. update \(q(L_{\cdot k})\) from the reconstruction residual that excludes factor \(k\);
      3. update \(q(F_{\cdot k})\) from the reconstruction residual, plus the survival term with weight \(\alpha_F\).
    3. Update \(\tau_j = n / \sum_i E_q(y_{ij} - \sum_k L_{ik}F_{jk})^2\).
    4. Compute the monitoring statistic \(J_r\) (Appendix A.8). After sweep 5, stop if \(|J_r - J_{r-1}| / |J_{r-1}| < \epsilon\).
  3. Fix the risk direction once from training data (Section 1.2.1).

Outputs: \(\bar L\), \(\bar F\), stored norms \(D_*\), \(\bar{\tilde\beta}\), \(\tau\). Prediction: for a new patient with data \(y_{\mathrm{new}}\) standardized within its own cohort and restricted to the measured training features \(\mathcal G\), \(\eta_{\mathrm{new}} = y_{\mathrm{new},\mathcal G}^\top\bar F_{\mathcal G}D_*^{-1}\bar{\tilde\beta}\), with every quantity fixed from training.

The evaluated fit used \(K = 7\), \(\alpha = 0.5\), \(\alpha_F = 0\), \(\epsilon = 10^{-5}\) and \(T = 300\), and met the stopping rule at sweep 20. The monitoring statistic \(J\) weights its reconstruction and survival components differently, evaluates the partial likelihood at the sweep’s starting predictor, and uses an approximate Kullback–Leibler (KL) bookkeeping for the activities (Appendix A.8). It is a stopping criterion, not the evidence lower bound (ELBO) of the joint model, and the updates are not guaranteed to increase it. The coefficient posterior variances stored with the evaluated fit are zero, so no coefficient uncertainty is reported for it.

1.2.1 Risk orientation

A concordance index requires the direction in which a score indicates higher risk. That direction must be fixed from training data alone; choosing it in each validation cohort from that cohort’s outcomes would bias the index upward. For the evaluated fit, higher \(\eta\) denotes longer survival, so the reported risk score is \(-\eta\), applied identically to every held-out cohort. On this risk scale the coefficient of Program 7 is \(+0.040\) and that of Program 3 is \(-0.012\).

1.3 Programs, starting rank, and classification

Three counts are kept apart. The starting rank \(K_{\mathrm{init}}\) is the number of factors at initialization. A factor is survival-active if \(|\bar{\tilde\beta}_k| > 0.001\). A factor that is not survival-active is genomics-only if its proportion of variance explained, \(\mathrm{PVE}_k = \lVert \bar L_{\cdot k}\rVert^2 \lVert \bar F_{\cdot k}\rVert^2 / \lVert Y \rVert_F^2\), exceeds 1%, and inactive otherwise. The retained programs are the survival-active and genomics-only factors together. In the single-modality model this classifies one fitted model: no factor is removed and nothing is refitted. Both thresholds are operational; the coefficient threshold was set from the observed scale of \(\tilde\beta\), and neither is a posterior probability.

The starting rank of 7 was first chosen by five-fold cross-validated training concordance with a one-standard-error rule: the best mean was at \(K = 8\) (0.651, standard error 0.026), and \(K = 7\) was the smallest rank within one standard error (0.633). It was retained after a sweep over \(K_{\mathrm{init}} = 2, \dots, 20\) in which the criteria disagreed and external concordance reached a plateau at 7 (Section 3.3). The choice therefore also used validation performance.

1.4 Training on multiple cohorts

The single-modality model fits one feature block pooled from two training cohorts on different platforms: The Cancer Genome Atlas pancreatic adenocarcinoma cohort (TCGA-PAAD) by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq; \(n = 144\)) and the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium cohort (CPTAC) by mass-spectrometry proteomics (\(n = 129\)). Genes are screened separately in each cohort by the combined mean-and-variance rank of DeSurv (Young et al., submitted), keeping the top 3,000 per cohort; the intersection has 2,064 genes. Each cohort is then standardized gene by gene to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Held-out cohorts receive the same within-cohort standardization and are scored on the training genes they measure. The model has optional cohort-specific components (cohort indicator columns in \(L\), a cohort-stratified baseline hazard, and cohort-specific coefficients); the evaluated configuration uses none of them.

1.5 Multimodal model

Reconstruction. For matched blocks \(m \in \{\mathrm{expr}, \mathrm{meth}\}\), \[ Y_m = \mathbf{1}\mu_m^\top + L F_m^\top + E_m, \qquad (E_m)_{ij} \sim N(0, \tau_{mj}^{-1}), \tag{4}\] with a feature intercept \(\mu_m\), shared nonnegative activities \(L\) with a point-exponential prior per factor, modality-specific signed loadings \(F_m\) with a point-Laplace prior \(g_{mk}\) for each modality and factor, and feature-specific precisions \(\tau_{mj}\). With an intercept, \(F_m\) describes deviations from each feature’s baseline and can take either sign, while \(L\) remains interpretable as program activity. Prior parameters for \(L\) and \(F_m\) are estimated by marginal likelihood after each column update, so a whole column can shrink to the point mass at zero.

Survival predictor. With \(\tilde Y_m = Y_m - \mathbf{1}\mu_m^\top\), the joint projection and predictor are \[ Z = \sum_m \tilde Y_m F_m, \qquad \eta_i = \sum_k Z_{ik}\beta_k, \qquad \beta_k \sim N(0, \sigma_k^2). \tag{5}\] The projection is not normalized. The map \((L_{\cdot k}, F_{mk}, \beta_k) \mapsto (c_k L_{\cdot k}, F_{mk}/c_k, c_k\beta_k)\) leaves both \(LF_m^\top\) and \(\eta\) unchanged, so the likelihood does not fix the scale of a factor. After every factor update the algorithm applies this map with \(c_k = \mathrm{sd}(\bar Z_{\cdot k})\), which sets the training standard deviation of each mean projection to 1, and transforms posterior moments and prior parameters consistently (Appendix B.9).

Updates. The loading update adds the reconstruction and Cox working terms with equal weight. Because the working term depends on the whole projection, features are coupled and are updated one at a time, with the projection moments refreshed after each. The coefficient update uses \(E(Z_{ik}^2) = \bar Z_{ik}^2 + \mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik})\), so loading uncertainty shrinks the coefficient. The working approximation is the diagonal one of Equation 3, written without the division by \(w_i\) and without a floor on \(w_i\). The intercept is updated to maximize the reconstruction likelihood, and the coordinate updates use centered projection moments. Appendix B gives the derivations.

Factor removal. Factors are removed using the score \[ \mathcal{S} = \sum_{m,j}\Big[\tfrac n2 \log\tfrac{\hat\tau_{mj}}{2\pi} - \tfrac{\hat\tau_{mj}}2 \sum_i E_q(\tilde y_{mij} - l_i^\top f_{mj})^2\Big] + \log \mathrm{PL}(\bar\eta) - \sum \mathrm{KL}, \tag{6}\] with \(\hat\tau\) at its maximum-likelihood value. The survival term is the partial log-likelihood at the posterior-mean predictor \(\bar\eta\), not its expectation under \(q\). The KL terms are those cached at each coordinate’s latest update, computed against the prior in force at that update; the priors are refitted afterwards without recomputing these penalties. After the coordinate loop, the change in \(\mathcal S\) from deleting each factor is computed with the other factors fixed and the intercept and precisions re-estimated. If a deletion does not lower \(\mathcal S\), the factor with the largest gain is removed and the model refitted, repeatedly. The check runs whether or not the loop converged. \(\mathcal S\) is an approximate removal score: neither the exact marginal likelihood nor an ELBO at the current posterior and priors is guaranteed to improve when a factor is deleted.

Classification. A factor is reconstruction-active if its share of the total centered sum of squares, \(\sum_m\lVert \bar L_{\cdot k}\bar F_{mk}^\top\rVert_F^2 / \sum_m\lVert\tilde Y_m\rVert_F^2\), is at least 1%, and survival-active if \(|\bar\beta_k|/\mathrm{sd}(\beta_k) \ge 1.96\). The 1.96 cutoff is an operational rule on the posterior mean and standard deviation, not an adjusted test. Classification is reported separately from removal.

Algorithm 2. Multimodal fit with factor removal, and prediction.

Inputs: training blocks \(Y_m\) on their measured scales; \((t_i, \delta_i)\); starting rank \(K_{\mathrm{init}}\); tolerance \(\epsilon\); outer cap \(T\); inner sweeps \(S\).

  1. Initialize \(\mu_m\) at the column means; \(\bar L\) and \(\bar F_m\) from the absolute leading singular vectors of the concatenated centered blocks; \(\tau_{mj}\) from the pooled variance of each block; and \(\bar\beta\) from a Cox fit on standardized initial projections, transformed back to the projection scale.
  2. For outer sweeps \(r = 1, \dots, T\):
    1. Re-estimate \(\mu_m\) and re-center \(\tilde Y_m\). Compute \(\bar Z\), \(\mathrm{Var}(Z)\), \(\bar\eta\), the working curvature \(w_i\) and the linear term \(h_i = u_i + w_i\bar\eta_i\). Hold \((w, h)\) fixed for this outer sweep.
    2. Repeat \(S\) inner sweeps; within each, for \(k = 1, \dots, K\):
      1. update \(q(L_{\cdot k})\) from both blocks’ reconstruction residuals, then refit its point-exponential prior;
      2. for each modality, update \(q(f_{mjk})\) one feature at a time from the reconstruction and survival terms, refreshing \(\bar Z_{\cdot k}\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Z_{\cdot k})\) after each feature, then refit the point-Laplace prior \(g_{mk}\);
      3. update \(q(\beta_k)\) by the normal-prior empirical-Bayes update with \(A = \sum_i w_i E(Z_{ik}^2)\) and \(B = \sum_i \bar Z_{ik}(h_i - w_i\bar\eta_{i,-k})\);
      4. rescale factor \(k\) so that \(\mathrm{sd}(\bar Z_{\cdot k}) = 1\).
    3. Update \(\tau_{mj} = n / \sum_i E_q(\tilde y_{mij} - l_i^\top f_{mj})^2\).
    4. Stop if, for each modality, the relative change in \(\bar L\bar F_m^\top\) and in \(\bar\eta\) is below \(\epsilon\).
  3. Compute the change in Equation 6 from deleting each factor. If the largest change is \(\ge 0\), delete that factor, return to step 2 from the remaining factors’ moments and priors, and repeat.

Outputs: posterior moments and priors, \(\mu_m\), \(\tau\), classification. Prediction: \(\eta_{\mathrm{new}} = \sum_m y_{m,\mathrm{new}}^\top\bar F_m\bar\beta\), with higher values denoting higher risk, a direction fixed before validation. Centering new data at the training intercept would change every score by the same constant and leave the concordance index unchanged.

The evaluated fits used \(\epsilon = 10^{-4}\), \(T = 500\) and \(S = 5\), point-Laplace loading priors in both modalities, and feature-specific precisions.

1.6 Approximations

Each coordinate update is exact for the quadratic working surrogate at fixed working quantities. The surrogate changes between sweeps, and its diagonal curvature replaces the coupled Cox Hessian. The single-modality monitoring statistic reweights its components, and the multimodal removal score evaluates survival at \(\bar\eta\) and uses cached KL penalties. Because the log partial likelihood is concave, the plug-in term \(\log\mathrm{PL}(\bar\eta)\) is an upper approximation to its posterior expectation; subtracting \(\frac12\sum_i w_i\mathrm{Var}(\eta_i)\) gives a variance-penalized alternative, but the full second-order correction would also involve the coupled Hessian and the covariance of \(\eta\) across patients. Neither algorithm is therefore exact coordinate ascent on one ELBO, and neither is guaranteed to increase its monitored quantity monotonically. Appendices A and B state each approximation beside the update it affects.

2 Evaluation

2.1 Data

Table 2 lists the training and validation cohorts. The matched multimodal cohorts contain TCGA and ICGC patients with both expression and methylation. Methylation is restricted to the 305,352 CpG sites present in both cohorts after removing sex-chromosome probes; missing values (0.07% in TCGA) are imputed within cohort by \(k\)-nearest neighbors. The multimodal fits use log2 expression and methylation \(\beta\)-values without standardization.

2.2 Simulation designs

Single-modality model, two cohorts. Each simulated dataset has two cohorts of 150 patients and 1,000 genes. True loading columns are the absolute values of loadings from an unsupervised empirical-Bayes matrix factorization (EBMF) of the real training data, scaled to amplitude 12; feature noise precisions are drawn from Gamma(2, 2). Survival times follow a Weibull proportional-hazards model whose predictor is \(\sum_k L_{ik}\beta_k\) over the shared programs (coefficients recycled from \(1.5, -1.2, 0.8, -0.5\)), with censoring calibrated to 30%. Cohort-specific programs have zero loadings outside their cohort and no survival effect. Three scenarios vary the structure: all shared (six shared programs), hybrid (two shared and two cohort-specific programs per cohort), and nothing shared (three cohort-specific programs per cohort and no prognostic program). Each dataset is split 75/25 into training and test patients, stratified by event status, giving 75 test patients. Two arms are fitted at starting ranks 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 and 20 with 15 datasets per setting (540 fits): the single-modality model with the evaluated settings, and a two-step arm consisting of a nonnegative EBMF (R package flashier, at most \(K_{\mathrm{init}}\) factors, with backfitting) followed by an unpenalized Cox model on least-squares projection scores. The data-generating predictor uses the latent activities \(L\), whereas both arms predict from projections.

Multimodal model. Each dataset has 120 training and 120 validation patients, 50 expression and 50 methylation features, and three true programs. Survival follows a Weibull model with predictor \(\sum_m Y_m F_m \beta\), matching the model’s predictor. Three scenarios set \(\beta\): two prognostic programs (\(0.70, 0.35, 0\)), one adverse and one protective program (\(0.70, -0.70, 0\)), and a low-variance prognostic program whose activities are scaled by 0.15 (\(\beta = 0, 0, 1.10\)). Feature noise precisions are drawn from Gamma(2, 2), and each feature’s noise standard deviation (SD) is multiplied by 1 (higher noise) or 0.25 (lower noise). Each feature is shifted by four noise SDs so that the data are nonnegative and the base model without intercepts can also be fitted. Starting ranks are 3 to 10 and 15, with three datasets per setting. Three variants are fitted to every dataset: a base model without feature intercepts or factor removal (nonnegative loadings, moment-based prior updates), the evaluated framework (Algorithm 2), and the same framework with the variance-penalized survival term in the removal score. The sweep contains 486 fits, 162 per variant.

2.3 Comparators

Principal single-modality comparator. An unsupervised EBMF (R package flashier; signed point-normal priors, gene-specific variances, greedy fitting with backfitting, at most 40 factors) of the same \(273 \times 2{,}064\) training matrix, followed by a Cox model with a least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) penalty on the normalized projection scores, with the penalty chosen by cross-validation (R package glmnet). The number of factors was not informed by the supervised model; 15 of the 40 factors received nonzero coefficients. Held-out patients are scored with the frozen loadings and coefficients.

Supporting single-modality comparators. A rank-matched two-step model (7 factors, unpenalized Cox) and a 20-factor two-step model with unpenalized Cox. Matching the rank gives the two-step model the supervised model’s choice of complexity, and the 20-factor model is not regularized, so neither is the principal comparison.

Multimodal comparators. On the matched cohorts, the same framework fitted to expression alone isolates the contribution of methylation. Three further arms are reported: the single-modality model of Section 1.2 applied to raw log2 TCGA expression, and two-step EBMF followed by unpenalized Cox on expression alone or on stacked expression and methylation.

2.4 Performance metrics and uncertainty

External performance is Harrell’s concordance index (C), with higher values indicating better discrimination and the risk direction fixed from training. Confidence intervals (CIs) are percentile bootstrap intervals over patients, with \(B = 2{,}000\) resamples for the single-modality comparisons and \(B = 1{,}000\) for the multimodal comparisons; differences resample patients jointly for both models. The intervals hold the fitted models fixed and do not include training uncertainty.

Three summaries of the single-modality comparison are not interchangeable. The mean external C averages five cohort C-indices. The concatenated difference, used for the principal and rank-matched comparisons, computes one C-index per model over all 616 patients, so comparable pairs can cross cohorts. The inverse-variance pooled difference, used for the 20-factor comparator, combines per-cohort paired differences. None is an equivalence or non-inferiority test.

Simulation summaries are means over datasets. In the single-modality simulation, test-set concordance is the outcome-oriented \(\max(C, 1-C)\), which is biased upward when there is no signal: in the nothing-shared scenario both arms score about 0.54. In the multimodal simulation, validation concordance uses the training-fixed direction. A true program counts as recovered when its absolute correlation with the best-matching estimated loading column is at least 0.7.

2.5 Biological characterization

The program labels in Section 4 come from the following analyses of the evaluated single-modality fit and of the starting-rank-7 multimodal fit.

  • Ranked enrichment. For each single-modality program, the 2,064 selected genes were ranked by their nonnegative posterior-mean loadings and tested against predefined gene sets with the fgsea algorithm for ranked gene-set enrichment (one-sided toward high loadings; set sizes 10–500). Collections were Hallmark, Reactome, the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), Gene Ontology biological process (GO-BP), and a PDAC collection of the Moffitt and Bailey subtype lists and the three DeSurv factor gene lists. The normalized enrichment score (NES) compares a set’s running-sum statistic with its permutation distribution; leading-edge genes are the set members ranked before the running-sum maximum. P-values were adjusted by the Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) method within each program and collection, and sets are reported at adjusted \(p < 0.10\). Over-representation analysis (ORA) of the top 50, 100 and 150 genes against the selected-gene background checked dependence on the cutoff. These analyses show which predefined sets are concentrated among a program’s highest-loading genes.
  • Subtype concordance and gene-list overlap. Training activities \(\bar L\) in TCGA (\(n = 144\)) were compared with the basal-like probability and calls of PurIST, a single-sample PDAC subtype classifier (Spearman correlation; Kruskal–Wallis test). The top 270 genes by loading were compared with the DeSurv factor lists, both restricted to the shared gene background (Jaccard similarity; hypergeometric test). P-values are unadjusted.
  • External signature association. For a selected set, the signature score is the mean within-cohort standardized expression of its leading-edge genes. A univariable Cox hazard ratio (HR) per unit of signature score was estimated in each external cohort. For the two genomics-only programs, the set was chosen after excluding the whole PDAC collection, a choice made after the first signature check for one of them scored a classical-tumor list. Signature scores are distinct from the frozen program projections used for survival curves, which group patients by within-cohort tertile and use cohort-stratified log-rank tests when cohorts are pooled.
  • Multimodal programs. Labels come from a manual reading of each program’s eight highest positive and six most negative expression loadings; no enrichment test or CpG annotation was performed. Each program’s share of a modality’s fitted signal is \(\lVert\bar L_{\cdot k}\rVert^2\lVert\bar F_{mk}\rVert^2\) divided by the sum of these rank-one squared norms within that modality. Correspondence with reference fits is the absolute Pearson correlation of loading columns over shared genes. Fourteen univariable Cox models (7 programs × 2 cohorts) give the HR per one within-cohort SD of the joint projection, without adjustment for multiplicity.

These analyses share inputs and are not independent validations. The PDAC collection and the gene-list overlap both use the DeSurv lists, and the selected gene universe was screened with DeSurv’s rule. The subtype check uses training activities in the cohort that trained the model. Multiplicity is controlled within each program and collection, not across them. The external control for the genomics-only programs was designed after an earlier result. The methods were chosen from those available, and whether they are the best tools for these questions has not been assessed.

3 Results

3.1 Single-modality simulation

At starting ranks at or above the true rank (6, 12 and 20), the model’s mean shared-program recovery was 97%–100% and its cohort-specific recovery 93%–100% (Table 3). Over-specifying the rank changed little. The two-step arm recovered fewer programs (73%–89% of shared and 70%–83% of specific programs) and did not change beyond rank 6, because its greedy factorization stopped adding factors. The model’s test concordance exceeded the two-step arm’s by 0.10–0.16 in the hybrid scenario from starting rank 3 upward and by about 0.02 in the all-shared scenario from rank 6 (Figure 1). At ranks 3 and 4 in the all-shared scenario the two-step arm was better by 0.02–0.03. With nothing prognostic, both arms were near the outcome-oriented null of 0.54. In the evaluated configuration the loading updates do not use survival, so these differences arise from the fitting procedure (initialization and coordinate updates versus greedy factorization) and the coefficient prior, not from survival-guided loadings. Among programs without a survival effect, 22%–35% were classified survival-active in the hybrid scenario at starting ranks 4–20, and 6%–10% with nothing shared.

A separate ten-dataset simulation tested cohort-specific coefficients for a program that is prognostic in only one cohort. The coefficient in the cohort with the effect exceeded the other cohort’s in 15 of 20 cohort-by-dataset cases at starting rank 6 and in 17 of 20 at rank 12 (medians 0.060 versus 0.008, and 0.054 versus 0.008); one dataset diverged, so medians are reported.

3.2 Single-modality external validation

The frozen model’s mean external C was 0.627 (from 0.549 in Moffitt to 0.657 in PACA-AU RNA-seq) and the principal comparator’s 0.601 (Table 4). Over the 616 concatenated patients, the C-indices were 0.6285 and 0.6026, a difference of 0.026 (95% CI 0.0002 to 0.050), so the advantage is small and its lower limit is close to zero. The rank-matched comparator, which was better in both PACA-AU cohorts, gave a difference of 0.011 (\(-0.013\) to \(0.033\)). The 20-factor unpenalized comparator gave an inverse-variance pooled difference of 0.042 (0.013 to 0.071).

Survival curves by within-cohort tertile of the frozen risk score generally favored the low-risk tertile (Figure 2). Log-rank tests indicated differences among tertiles in three of five cohorts: Dijk (\(p = 0.00046\)), PACA-AU RNA-seq (\(p = 0.021\)) and Puleo (\(p < 0.0001\)), but not PACA-AU microarray (\(p = 0.075\)) or Moffitt (\(p = 0.17\)). Tertiles are descriptive within-cohort groups, not clinical cutoffs.

3.3 Starting rank and factor classification

At starting rank 7 the evaluated fit has three inactive factors, two genomics-only programs (5 and 6), and two survival-active programs (3 and 7); the retained programs each explain 1.9%–3.0% of the training variance. In the sweep over starting ranks (Table 5), the monitoring statistic and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) both favor \(K_{\mathrm{init}} = 3\), the cross-validated survival log partial likelihood is highest at 19, and the joint log-likelihood (not shown) keeps rising to 15. External concordance is below 0.60 up to starting rank 6 and between 0.626 and 0.628 at every rank from 7 to 20 except 11 (0.600) and 13 (0.539). The number of survival-active programs is 1 at starting ranks 2–4 and 2 or 3 from rank 5 upward. Starting rank 7 is the smallest rank on the external-concordance plateau and the rank selected by training cross-validation.

At starting rank 7 the classification (two survival-active, two genomics-only) is unchanged for coefficient thresholds from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-2}\) combined with PVE thresholds from 0.1% to 2%. A PVE threshold of 5% removes both genomics-only programs; a coefficient threshold of 0 counts four programs as survival-active, because two coefficients are of order \(10^{-10}\); and a threshold of 0.05 counts none.

3.4 Multimodal simulation

With factor removal, the final number of programs depends much less on the starting rank (Figure 3); the base model has no removal step, so its final rank equals the starting rank in all 162 fits. At lower noise, the evaluated framework returned a mean of 3.2–3.3 programs in the two scenarios with high-variance prognostic programs and 2.5 in the low-variance scenario, averaged over starting ranks, and the means were close to constant from starting rank 4 upward. At higher noise it returned fewer than three programs on average (1.7–2.0), and the final rank rose with the starting rank, from 1 at starting rank 3 to 2.3–3.3 at ranks 10 and 15. All 162 fits of the evaluated framework met the convergence criterion, against 27 of 162 for the base model.

At lower noise the framework recovered all three programs in the two-prognostic scenario and 2.96 of 3 in the adverse-and-protective scenario, found 87% of prognostic programs with the correct sign, and had validation C of 0.79–0.80 (Table 6). In the low-variance scenario it recovered about two programs, found the low-variance prognostic program in none of the 27 fits, and classified 1.26 other programs per fit as survival-active, attributing survival to high-variance programs; validation C was 0.63. At higher noise, recovery was lower (0.93–1.33 programs), but the low-variance prognostic program was found in 52% of fits (48% with the correct sign). In that setting every true program is weak, so the result does not show recovery of a low-variance program alongside strong ones. The variance-penalized survival term changed no summary in Table 6 by more than 0.04. Each cell averages 27 fits from three simulated datasets per setting, which limits precision.

3.5 Multimodal real-data validation

On the 50 primary-PDAC ICGC donors at starting rank 7, the joint expression-and-methylation fit had \(C = 0.685\) (0.579, 0.779) and the expression-only fit of the same framework \(C = 0.676\) (0.569, 0.770) (Table 7). Neither fit met the convergence criterion within 500 sweeps. The difference of 0.010 is small relative to either interval and was not tested; similar observed concordance is not evidence of equivalence. On all 67 donors the order reversed (0.639 and 0.653). The two-step comparators had concordance below 0.53, and the base joint model without intercepts or factor removal 0.453.

No factor was removed at any starting rank: the final rank equals the starting rank in all nine fits (Table 8). Only the fits at starting ranks 3 and 4 met the convergence criterion; the other seven stopped at the cap, and the removal check ran on those unconverged fits. Concordance on the 50 primary donors ranged from 0.500 at rank 5, where no program was survival-active and every patient received the same score, to 0.685 at rank 7; the median over the nine ranks was 0.572. The number of survival-active programs rose with the starting rank, from 0 to 11, while concordance did not. Rank 7 was chosen in advance as the single-modality default, but it is also the rank with the highest validation concordance in this sweep, so the rank-7 results are favorable relative to the other ranks. The reconstruction term of Equation 6 sums over \(144 \times 13{,}000\) molecular values, whereas the survival term is a partial likelihood over 75 deaths, so survival can have little influence on which programs are retained.

4 Biological findings

4.1 Single-modality programs

The evaluated fit retains four programs (Table 9). Their loadings were estimated without survival (\(\alpha_F = 0\)), so the labels describe dominant expression structure of the training data that survival then weights; they are not evidence of survival-guided discovery. Normalized enrichment scores for the cited sets are modest (1.05–1.29), and multiplicity is controlled only within each program and collection.

Program 7: adverse, basal-like. Its highest loadings combine glycolytic genes (GAPDH, ENO1, TPI1, PGK1, LDHA) with integrin and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) genes (ITGA3, ITGB4, MET, CDCP1). Enriched sets include DeSurv’s basal-like list (adjusted \(p = 0.0006\)), the KEGG growth-factor RTK–phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and RAS–extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathways (adjusted \(p = 0.001\)), and the Bailey squamous list (adjusted \(p = 0.03\)). Training activities correlate with the PurIST basal-like probability (\(\rho = 0.58\)); the top genes overlap only DeSurv’s basal-like list (Jaccard 0.18); the basal-like signature has an HR above 1 in all five external cohorts (1.30–2.40 per unit of signature score, \(p < 0.05\) in two); and projection tertiles separate external survival (Figure 4). The program corresponds to a factor of the unsupervised factorization of the same data (\(r = 0.69\); next best 0.33).

Program 3: protective, classical. The top genes are epithelial and secretory (CAPN5, LPCAT4, MLPH, SLC45A3, TJP3, GALNT6). The classical label rests mainly on subtype concordance (\(\rho = -0.58\) with the basal-like probability) and on the classical signature’s HR below 1 in all five cohorts (0.42–0.88, \(p < 0.05\) in three). The enrichment is less specific: DeSurv’s classical and basal-like lists are both enriched (adjusted \(p = 0.017\) each), together with the Moffitt classical list and three integrin–focal adhesion kinase sets, and the top genes overlap both lists (Jaccard 0.13 and 0.10). Its unsupervised correspondence is less distinct (\(r = -0.72\); next best 0.60).

Program 5: genomics-only, desmoplastic stroma. Collagen and fibroblast genes dominate (COL1A2, COL3A1, COL5A2, THBS2, CDH11, SPARC). Its twelve enriched sets are led by the Hallmark epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) set (adjusted \(p = 0.0005\)), DeSurv’s stromal-immune list and extracellular matrix (ECM) organization. Its top genes overlap only the stromal-immune list (Jaccard 0.18), it leans weakly basal (\(\rho = 0.30\)), and its EMT signature is not consistently prognostic externally (HR 0.73–1.50, \(p < 0.05\) in one cohort).

Program 6: genomics-only, immune infiltrate with a vascular component. Lymphoid genes (IKZF1, AKNA, IL10RA, RCSD1, PREX1) are mixed with vascular and basement-membrane genes (APOLD1, COL14A1, TNXB, FBLN5, SLIT3, SPARCL1). Most of its 40 enriched sets are immune GO-BP terms, although the two smallest adjusted p-values belong to DeSurv’s classical and stromal-immune lists. It is uncorrelated with the PurIST axis (\(\rho = -0.03\)) but differs across PurIST calls (Kruskal–Wallis \(p = 0.007\)), a non-monotonic relation. Scored on its own immune set, it has no consistent external association (HR 0.53–1.39, none with \(p < 0.05\)).

Together, the four programs correspond to DeSurv’s three factors, with DeSurv’s combined stromal-immune factor divided between a stromal and an immune program. This is gene-list correspondence within a gene universe screened by DeSurv’s rule, not an independent replication of DeSurv and not a predictive comparison with it.

Adverse and protective labels follow the marginal association of each program’s projection with survival. On the risk scale, the coefficients of Programs 7 (\(+0.040\)) and 3 (\(-0.012\)) agree in sign with these labels. The coefficients are conditional on the other programs and are not interchangeable with the marginal associations.

4.2 Multimodal programs

The starting-rank-7 joint fit has seven programs (Table 10). Labels are provisional. They come from a manual reading of each program’s highest positive and most negative expression loadings, together with loading correlations to three reference fits. No enrichment test and no CpG annotation was performed. The correlations are absolute values, so they do not show whether a matched pair points in the same direction, and best matches chosen independently for each program need not form a one-to-one alignment; for example, both the immune and stromal programs have their best single-modality match in Program 6.

The one survival-active program (4) is the basal-like versus classical axis. Its marginal HR per SD of the joint projection is 1.99 in ICGC (\(p = 0.00033\)) and 1.34 in TCGA (\(p = 0.0055\)). It corresponds to single-modality Program 7 (\(|r| = 0.68\)), and the classical/gastric program (1) corresponds to single-modality Program 3 (\(|r| = 0.79\)), although Program 1 is not survival-active here. Of the 14 marginal tests, three have \(p < 0.05\) (Program 4 in both cohorts and Program 5 in TCGA), without correction for multiplicity.

Methylation contributes in two ways (Figure 5). A methylation-only program carries 58.9% of the fitted methylation signal and has no expression loading. The immune program carries 20.9% of the methylation signal while being defined on the expression side by immune genes. Neither is survival-active, and neither has a marginal association with \(p < 0.05\). The basal-like program carries 4.5% of the methylation signal. These shares describe the fitted rank-one reconstruction within each modality; they are not additive proportions of variance, because cross-terms between programs are excluded, and they do not measure contributions to survival prediction.

The evidence therefore supports expression-defined program labels and the existence of methylation-dominant structure among the screened CpG sites, but not what that structure is. The 10,000 CpG sites were chosen by variance, and high-variance CpG sites often track cell composition, so the immune and methylation-only programs may reflect composition or technical variation. This is an explanation to test, not a finding.

5 Discussion

5.1 Interpretation and implications

The single-modality model produces a small number of interpretable programs and a risk score that transfers across expression and proteomic platforms. Its four retained programs correspond to the basal-like and classical tumor axes and to stromal and immune components that are well described in PDAC, and the score separates survival in held-out cohorts measured on platforms not used in training. Its advantage over an independently tuned two-step pipeline is small: 0.026 in concatenated concordance, with a lower confidence limit near zero, and no advantage over a rank-matched two-step model. The concatenated estimand also includes comparisons across cohorts, so it does not establish a within-cohort advantage. In the evaluated configuration survival does not enter the loading updates, so the advantage reflects how programs are fitted and coefficients shrunk rather than survival-guided discovery of programs. That the model nonetheless finds recognizable biology from the dominant structure of the data is useful for interpretation but does not yet show what survival supervision adds.

The multimodal framework solves a specific problem of the base multimodal model, which could not remove unneeded factors: with intercepts, signed loadings and marginal-likelihood prior estimation, it returns close to the true rank in simulation when the true programs explain enough variance, and every simulated fit converges. On real data it adds molecular structure, a methylation-dominant program and methylation loading on an immune program, but no demonstrated improvement in prediction. The framework did not recover a planted low-variance prognostic program at lower noise. The single-modality loading update receives no survival information, so its evaluated configuration does not test whether survival supervision improves recovery of such programs. That question, which motivates supervised factorization, remains open.

5.2 Limitations

Several features of the fitted models limit the conclusions. The evaluated single-modality fit has no stored coefficient uncertainty. Both algorithms rely on a diagonal working approximation to the Cox partial likelihood, and their stopping and removal criteria are approximations: the single-modality monitoring statistic weights its components unequally and uses an approximate KL term for the activities, and the multimodal removal score evaluates survival at the posterior-mean predictor and uses KL penalties computed against earlier priors. How these approximations affect the stopping point and the selected rank has not been assessed. Most real multimodal fits did not converge, no factor was removed on real data, and survival has little weight in the removal score relative to reconstruction.

The evidence is also limited by the data and evaluation. The multimodal results rest on one training cohort of 144 patients with 75 deaths and a 50-donor validation set, so concordance intervals are wide (about \(\pm 0.10\)), and rank 7 is favorable among the starting ranks evaluated. The external cohorts differ in platform, size and event rate; two come from the same ICGC project, and the matched multimodal validation set overlaps one of them. Bootstrap intervals hold the fitted models fixed. The single-modality starting rank was informed by external concordance. Feature screening keeps 3,000 genes and about 3% of the available CpG sites, and the effect of that choice is unknown. The single-modality simulation reports outcome-oriented concordance, and the multimodal simulation uses three datasets per setting. The biological characterization uses analyses that share inputs, includes a correction designed after an earlier result and a within-training subtype check, reports unadjusted tests and unsigned correspondence for the multimodal programs, and relies on methods whose suitability has not been assessed.

5.3 Continuing work

The configuration with \(\alpha_F = 0\) is not the intended final method. A supervised factorization should be able to find a prognostic program that explains little molecular variance, and survival cannot help the loading updates select such a program unless it enters them. The continuing work has five aims.

  1. Survival supervision of the loadings. Determine why survival has little effect even when it enters the loading update. Its contribution is multiplied by the current coefficient, so a direction that no program already points along receives no survival information; its precision is small relative to the reconstruction term; and in the single-modality model the loading scale is not fixed during the update. The aim is a supervised loading update that recovers a planted low-variance prognostic program in most simulated datasets, without instability and without loss of external concordance.
  2. Projection scale and prediction. Settle the definition of the projection and the units of the coefficients under a common scale convention for both models, and carry the chosen supervision method into the multimodal model.
  3. Rank selection. Develop a rule that accounts for both survival and reconstruction without using validation outcomes, and evaluate it with replicated simulations for both models.
  4. Robustness and comparators. Assess sensitivity to initialization, loading prior family and the numbers of genes and CpG sites, and compare the final method with unsupervised factorization, the two-step pipeline and DeSurv on the same training and validation data.
  5. Biology of the final programs. Characterize the final programs, including sign-aware enrichment of multimodal loadings, annotation of the CpG sites, and tests of cell-composition and technical explanations for the methylation-dominant structure.

Appendix A. Single-modality derivations

This appendix starts from the likelihood, priors and variational family of the single-modality model and derives, for each coordinate, the pseudo-observation \(x = B/A\) and standard error \(s = A^{-1/2}\) passed to the empirical-Bayes normal-means (EBNM) solver. It then states where the evaluated algorithm departs from the joint target. Throughout, \(\bar\theta = E_q\theta\) and \(\overline{\theta^2} = E_q\theta^2\) for the variational posterior \(q\), and \(E_{-\theta}\) denotes expectation under \(q\) over every coordinate except \(\theta\).

A.1 Model, target and evaluated algorithm

Reconstruction likelihood. With \(e_{ij} \sim N(0, \tau_j^{-1})\) in Equation 1, \[ \ell_Y = \sum_{i,j}\Big\{\tfrac12\log\frac{\tau_j}{2\pi} - \frac{\tau_j}{2}\Big(y_{ij} - \sum_k L_{ik}F_{jk}\Big)^2\Big\}. \tag{7}\]

Cox partial likelihood. Let \(s_1 < s_2 < \cdots\) be the distinct death times, \(\mathcal D_a\) the patients who die at \(s_a\), \(d_a = |\mathcal D_a|\), and \(\mathcal R_a = \{i : t_i \ge s_a\}\) the risk set. With Breslow’s handling of ties, \[ \ell_C(\eta) = \sum_a\Big\{\sum_{i\in\mathcal D_a}\eta_i - d_a\log\sum_{i\in\mathcal R_a}e^{\eta_i}\Big\}. \tag{8}\] The partial likelihood is not a full likelihood for the survival times; using it as the survival term defines a partial-likelihood joint target rather than a fully specified generative model.

Priors. \(L_{ik} \sim g_{L,k}\) and \(F_{jk} \sim g_{F,k}\), each a point mass at zero mixed with an exponential distribution, and \(\tilde\beta_k \sim g_{\beta,k} = N(0, \sigma_k^2)\), all independent. The residual precisions \(\tau_j\) and the prior parameters are point estimates.

Joint target. In the target, the predictor uses the random loadings, \(\eta_i = \sum_k\tilde\beta_k\sum_j y_{ij}F_{jk}/d_k(F)\) with \(d_k(F) = \lVert F_{\cdot k}\rVert_2\). With the mean-field family \[ q(L, F, \tilde\beta) = \prod_{i,k} q(L_{ik})\prod_{j,k} q(F_{jk})\prod_k q(\tilde\beta_k), \] the variational objective is \[ \mathcal L(q) = E_q\ell_Y + E_q\ell_C(\eta) - \sum_{i,k}\mathrm{KL}\big(q(L_{ik})\,\Vert\, g_{L,k}\big) - \sum_{j,k}\mathrm{KL}\big(q(F_{jk})\,\Vert\, g_{F,k}\big) - \sum_k\mathrm{KL}\big(q(\tilde\beta_k)\,\Vert\, g_{\beta,k}\big). \tag{9}\]

Evaluated algorithm. Two features make the evaluated algorithm differ from coordinate ascent on Equation 9. First, at the start of sweep \(r\) it fixes \(D^{(r)} = \mathrm{diag}(\lVert\bar F^{(r-1)}_{\cdot k}\rVert_2)\) and the projection \(\tilde Z^{(r)} = Y\bar F^{(r-1)}[D^{(r)}]^{-1}\) and treats \(\tilde Z\) as a known covariate matrix for the rest of the sweep, so the coefficient update has no projection variance. Second, \(E_q\ell_C\) is replaced by the expectation of the working quadratic of A.2. \(L\) does not enter \(\eta\) in either the target or the algorithm.

A.2 Cox working approximation

Let \(\hat\eta\) be the predictor at the start of a sweep and \[ P_{ai} = \frac{\mathbf 1\{i\in\mathcal R_a\}\,e^{\hat\eta_i}}{\sum_{l\in\mathcal R_a}e^{\hat\eta_l}}, \] the share of risk-set member \(i\) at death time \(s_a\).

Score. Differentiating Equation 8, \(\partial\big(d_a\log\sum_{l\in\mathcal R_a}e^{\eta_l}\big)/\partial\eta_i = d_aP_{ai}\), so \[ u_i = \frac{\partial\ell_C}{\partial\eta_i}\Big|_{\hat\eta} = \delta_i - \sum_a d_aP_{ai}. \] The Breslow cumulative baseline hazard is \(\hat H_0(t) = \sum_{a: s_a\le t}d_a/\sum_{l\in\mathcal R_a}e^{\hat\eta_l}\). Because \(i \in \mathcal R_a\) exactly when \(s_a \le t_i\), \[ a_i \equiv e^{\hat\eta_i}\hat H_0(t_i) = \sum_a d_aP_{ai}, \qquad u_i = \delta_i - a_i . \]

Exact curvature. Differentiating again, \(\partial^2\big(d_a\log\sum_{l\in\mathcal R_a}e^{\eta_l}\big)/\partial\eta_i\partial\eta_h = d_a(P_{ai}\mathbf 1\{i = h\} - P_{ai}P_{ah})\), so the negative Hessian is \[ \mathcal H = \sum_a d_a\big\{\mathrm{diag}(P_a) - P_aP_a^\top\big\}, \qquad \mathcal H_{ii} = \sum_a d_aP_{ai}(1 - P_{ai}) = a_i - \sum_a d_aP_{ai}^2 . \] \(\mathcal H\) couples patients through shared risk sets, and its diagonal is smaller than \(a_i\).

Working replacement. The algorithm keeps the exact score and replaces \(\mathcal H\) by \(W = \mathrm{diag}(w)\) with \(w_i = \max(a_i, 10^{-6})\), a Poisson-style working curvature. The resulting surrogate is \[ \ell_C(\eta) \approx \ell_C(\hat\eta) + \sum_i u_i(\eta_i - \hat\eta_i) - \tfrac12\sum_i w_i(\eta_i - \hat\eta_i)^2 . \] Expanding \((\eta_i - \hat\eta_i)^2 = \eta_i^2 - 2\eta_i\hat\eta_i + \hat\eta_i^2\) and collecting terms that do not involve \(\eta\) into a constant \(c\), \[ \ell_C(\eta) \approx c + \sum_i\Big\{(u_i + w_i\hat\eta_i)\eta_i - \tfrac12 w_i\eta_i^2\Big\}. \tag{10}\] For \(w_i > 0\), completing the square with \(z_i = \hat\eta_i + u_i/w_i\) gives \((u_i + w_i\hat\eta_i)\eta_i - \frac12w_i\eta_i^2 = w_iz_i\eta_i - \frac12w_i\eta_i^2 = -\frac12w_i(z_i - \eta_i)^2 + \frac12w_iz_i^2\), so \[ \ell_C(\eta) \approx c' - \tfrac12\sum_i w_i(z_i - \eta_i)^2 . \tag{11}\] At the floor, \(w_i = 10^{-6}\) while \(u_i = \delta_i - a_i\) is retained. When risk sets are stratified, \(P_{ai}\) and \(\hat H_0\) are formed within strata; the evaluated fit has no strata. The surrogate is a working approximation, not the second-order Taylor expansion of \(\ell_C\).

A.3 Reduction to empirical-Bayes normal means

For one scalar coordinate \(\theta\) with prior \(g\), the optimal mean-field factor satisfies \[ \log q^*(\theta) = E_{-\theta}\big[\text{log likelihood terms}\big] + \log g(\theta) + c . \] In every update below, the expected likelihood terms are quadratic in \(\theta\), \(B\theta - \frac12A\theta^2 + c\) with \(A > 0\). Completing the square, \[ B\theta - \tfrac12A\theta^2 = -\tfrac12A\Big(\theta - \frac BA\Big)^2 + \frac{B^2}{2A}, \] so \[ q^*(\theta) \propto N(x;\, \theta, s^2)\,g(\theta), \qquad x = B/A, \quad s = A^{-1/2}. \tag{12}\] This is the posterior of \(\theta\) given one Gaussian observation \(x\) with standard error \(s\). When \(H\) coordinates \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_H\) share a prior, the prior is estimated by maximizing the marginal likelihood of their pseudo-observations, \[ \hat g = \arg\max_g\sum_{h=1}^H\log p_g(x_h), \qquad p_g(x_h) = \int N(x_h;\, \theta, s_h^2)\,g(d\theta), \] and each \(q(\theta_h)\) is the posterior under \(\hat g\).

KL identity. For the posterior under the same prior, \(q(\theta) = N(x; \theta, s^2)g(\theta)/p_g(x)\), so \(\log q(\theta) - \log g(\theta) = \log N(x; \theta, s^2) - \log p_g(x)\) and \[ \mathrm{KL}(q\,\Vert\,g) = E_q\log N(x;\, \theta, s^2) - \log p_g(x). \tag{13}\] For a vector of \(H\) coordinates with a common precision \(A\), \[ \sum_h E_q\log N(x_h;\, \theta_h, A^{-1}) = \frac H2\log\frac{A}{2\pi} - \frac A2\sum_h\big(x_h^2 - 2x_h\bar\theta_h + \overline{\theta_h^2}\big). \tag{14}\] If \(A = B = 0\) the coordinate receives no information and \(q = g\). The implementation instead floors each \(A\) at \(10^{-10}\), which gives a very large \(s\) and a posterior indistinguishable from the prior.

A.4 Posteriors under point-mass priors

Point-exponential prior. Let \(g = (1-\pi)\delta_0 + \pi\,\lambda e^{-\lambda\theta}\mathbf 1\{\theta > 0\}\). For the slab, expand the exponent and complete the square with \(m = x - \lambda s^2\): \[ -\frac{(\theta - x)^2}{2s^2} - \lambda\theta = -\frac{(\theta - m)^2}{2s^2} - \lambda x + \frac{\lambda^2 s^2}{2}, \] which follows from \(m^2 - x^2 = -2\lambda s^2x + \lambda^2s^4\). Hence \(N(x; \theta, s^2)\lambda e^{-\lambda\theta} = \lambda\exp(-\lambda x + \lambda^2s^2/2)\,N(\theta; m, s^2)\), and integrating over \(\theta > 0\) gives \(\lambda\exp(-\lambda x + \lambda^2s^2/2)\,\Phi(m/s)\). The marginal likelihood and posterior weights are therefore \[ p_g(x) = (1-\pi)N(x;\, 0, s^2) + \pi\lambda e^{-\lambda x + \lambda^2s^2/2}\,\Phi(m/s), \qquad \omega_0 = \frac{(1-\pi)N(x; 0, s^2)}{p_g(x)}, \quad \omega_+ = 1 - \omega_0, \] and the posterior is \(\omega_0\delta_0\) plus \(\omega_+\) times \(N(m, s^2)\) truncated to \((0, \infty)\).

Truncated-normal moments. Write \(\theta = m + s\zeta\) with \(\zeta\) standard normal conditioned on \(\zeta > -a\), \(a = m/s\), and let \(r = \phi(a)/\Phi(a)\). Using \(\int_{-a}^\infty \zeta\phi(\zeta)\,d\zeta = \phi(a)\) and, by parts, \(\int_{-a}^\infty\zeta^2\phi(\zeta)\,d\zeta = \Phi(a) - a\phi(a)\), we have \(E\zeta = r\) and \(E\zeta^2 = 1 - ar\). Hence \[ M_+(m) = E\theta = m + sr, \qquad S_+(m) = E\theta^2 = m^2 + 2msr + s^2(1 - ar) = m^2 + s^2 + msr, \tag{15}\] and the posterior moments are \(\bar\theta = \omega_+M_+(m)\) and \(\overline{\theta^2} = \omega_+S_+(m)\). For large negative \(a\), \(\log\Phi(a)\) and \(r\) are evaluated with tail approximations for numerical stability. The point-Laplace case used in the multimodal model is derived in Appendix B.6.

A.5 Coefficient update

Fix \(k\) and write \(a_i = \tilde Z_{ik}\), which is a known covariate within the sweep, and \(H_i = \sum_{l\ne k}\tilde Z_{il}\tilde\beta_l\), which does not involve \(\tilde\beta_k\). Then \(\eta_i = H_i + a_i\tilde\beta_k\). The survival weight \(\alpha\) multiplies the working term Equation 11, so the terms involving \(\tilde\beta_k\) are \(-\frac{\alpha}{2}\sum_iw_i(z_i - H_i - a_i\tilde\beta_k)^2\). Expanding the square, \[ (z_i - H_i - a_i\tilde\beta_k)^2 = (z_i - H_i)^2 - 2a_i\tilde\beta_k(z_i - H_i) + a_i^2\tilde\beta_k^2, \] and taking \(E_{-\tilde\beta_k}\), under which \(E(z_i - H_i) = z_i - \bar H_i\) and \(E(z_i - H_i)^2\) is a constant \(c_i\), \[ E_{-\tilde\beta_k}(z_i - H_i - a_i\tilde\beta_k)^2 = c_i - 2a_i\tilde\beta_k(z_i - \bar H_i) + a_i^2\tilde\beta_k^2 . \] Multiplying by \(-\alpha w_i/2\) and summing over \(i\), \[ \tilde\beta_k\,\alpha\sum_iw_ia_i(z_i - \bar H_i) - \tfrac12\tilde\beta_k^2\,\alpha\sum_iw_ia_i^2 + c, \] so \[ A_{\beta,k} = \alpha\sum_iw_i\tilde Z_{ik}^2, \qquad B_{\beta,k} = \alpha\sum_iw_i\tilde Z_{ik}(z_i - \bar H_i), \qquad x_{\beta,k} = \frac{\sum_iw_i\tilde Z_{ik}(z_i - \bar H_i)}{\sum_iw_i\tilde Z_{ik}^2}, \qquad s_{\beta,k} = A_{\beta,k}^{-1/2}. \tag{16}\] For \(\alpha > 0\) the pseudo-observation does not depend on \(\alpha\), and the standard error is inflated by \(\alpha^{-1/2}\) (\(\sqrt 2\) at \(\alpha = 0.5\)), provided the floor on \(A\) is inactive. In the joint target with random loadings, \(\tilde Z_{ik}^2\) would be replaced by \(E(\tilde Z_{ik}^2)\); the plug-in projection does not pass loading uncertainty to the coefficient.

Normal prior. With \(g_{\beta,k} = N(0, \sigma^2)\) the marginal distribution of \(x\) is \(N(0, s^2 + \sigma^2)\), with log-likelihood \[ \ell(\sigma^2) = -\tfrac12\log\{2\pi(s^2 + \sigma^2)\} - \frac{x^2}{2(s^2 + \sigma^2)}, \qquad \ell'(\sigma^2) = \frac{x^2 - (s^2 + \sigma^2)}{2(s^2 + \sigma^2)^2}. \] The derivative is positive for \(\sigma^2 < x^2 - s^2\) and negative beyond, so the maximizer over \(\sigma^2 \ge 0\) is \[ \hat\sigma_k^2 = \max(0,\, x^2 - s^2). \] For \(\hat\sigma_k^2 > 0\), completing the square in \(N(x; \tilde\beta, s^2)N(\tilde\beta; 0, \hat\sigma^2)\) gives precision \(s^{-2} + \hat\sigma^{-2}\), so \[ \bar{\tilde\beta}_k = \frac{x\,\hat\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2 + s^2}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\tilde\beta_k) = \frac{\hat\sigma^2s^2}{\hat\sigma^2 + s^2}. \] If \(|x| \le s\), then \(\hat\sigma_k^2 = 0\) and \(q(\tilde\beta_k)\) is the point mass at zero.

A.6 Activity update

\(L\) appears only in \(\ell_Y\). Define the random residual excluding factor \(k\), \(r_{ij}^{(-k)} = y_{ij} - \sum_{l\ne k}L_{il}F_{jl}\), and its mean \(R_{ij}^{(-k)} = E_q r_{ij}^{(-k)} = y_{ij} - \sum_{l\ne k}\bar L_{il}\bar F_{jl}\), which uses the independence of \(L_{il}\) and \(F_{jl}\) under \(q\). The terms of Equation 7 involving \(L_{ik}\) are \(-\frac{\tau_j}{2}(r_{ij}^{(-k)} - L_{ik}F_{jk})^2\). Expanding, \[ (r_{ij}^{(-k)} - L_{ik}F_{jk})^2 = (r_{ij}^{(-k)})^2 - 2L_{ik}r_{ij}^{(-k)}F_{jk} + L_{ik}^2F_{jk}^2 . \] Under \(q\), \(F_{jk}\) is independent of \(r_{ij}^{(-k)}\), which involves only the other factors, so \[ E_{-L_{ik}}(r_{ij}^{(-k)} - L_{ik}F_{jk})^2 = c_{ij} - 2L_{ik}R_{ij}^{(-k)}\bar F_{jk} + L_{ik}^2\overline{F_{jk}^2}. \] Multiplying by \(-\tau_j/2\) and summing over \(j\), \[ A_{L,k} = \sum_j\tau_j\overline{F_{jk}^2}, \qquad B_{L,ik} = \sum_j\tau_jR_{ij}^{(-k)}\bar F_{jk}, \qquad x_{L,ik} = B_{L,ik}/A_{L,k}, \qquad s_{L,k} = A_{L,k}^{-1/2}. \tag{17}\] All \(n\) pseudo-observations of factor \(k\) share the precision \(A_{L,k}\). The point-exponential prior \(g_{L,k}\) is fitted by maximizing their joint marginal likelihood (A.3), and the posterior moments follow from A.4. Because \(\eta\) does not depend on \(L\), this update holds in every configuration of the model.

A.7 Loading update

Reconstruction terms. Exchanging the roles of \(L\) and \(F\) in A.6, the terms of Equation 7 involving \(F_{jk}\) are \(-\frac{\tau_j}{2}\sum_i(r_{ij}^{(-k)} - L_{ik}F_{jk})^2\), and \[ E_{-F_{jk}}(r_{ij}^{(-k)} - L_{ik}F_{jk})^2 = c_{ij} - 2F_{jk}R_{ij}^{(-k)}\bar L_{ik} + F_{jk}^2\overline{L_{ik}^2}. \] Multiplying by \(-\tau_j/2\) and summing over \(i\), \[ A^{\mathrm{rec}}_{F,jk} = \tau_j\sum_i\overline{L_{ik}^2}, \qquad B^{\mathrm{rec}}_{F,jk} = \tau_j\sum_iR_{ij}^{(-k)}\bar L_{ik}. \tag{18}\]

Survival terms of the target, with a fixed normalizer. If \(d_k\) depends on \(F\), \(\eta_i\) is not linear in \(F_{jk}\) and the working term is not quadratic in it. Holding \(d_k\) fixed, set \(a_{ij} = y_{ij}/d_k\), \(C_i = \sum_{h\ne j}a_{ih}F_{hk}\) and \(H_i = \eta_{i,-k}\), so that \(\eta_i = H_i + \tilde\beta_k(C_i + a_{ij}F_{jk})\). With \(G_i = z_i - H_i - \tilde\beta_kC_i\), \[ (z_i - \eta_i)^2 = G_i^2 - 2a_{ij}F_{jk}\tilde\beta_kG_i + a_{ij}^2\tilde\beta_k^2F_{jk}^2 . \] Under \(q\), \(\tilde\beta_k\), \(H_i\) and \(C_i\) are independent of each other and of \(F_{jk}\), so \(E(\tilde\beta_kG_i) = \bar{\tilde\beta}_k(z_i - \bar H_i) - \overline{\tilde\beta_k^2}\,\bar C_i\). Multiplying the expectation by \(-w_i/2\) and summing over \(i\) gives the coefficients \[ A^{\mathrm{surv}}_{F,jk} = \overline{\tilde\beta_k^2}\sum_iw_i\frac{y_{ij}^2}{d_k^2}, \qquad B^{\mathrm{surv}}_{F,jk} = \bar{\tilde\beta}_k\sum_iw_i\frac{y_{ij}}{d_k}(z_i - \bar H_i) - \overline{\tilde\beta_k^2}\sum_iw_i\frac{y_{ij}}{d_k}\bar C_i . \tag{19}\] The last term couples feature \(j\) to the other features of factor \(k\) through \(\bar C_i\).

Implemented update. The implementation combines the reconstruction terms with a simpler survival branch, using weights \(1 - \alpha_F\) and \(\alpha_F\): \[ A_{F,jk} = (1-\alpha_F)A^{\mathrm{rec}}_{F,jk} + \alpha_F\overline{\tilde\beta_k^2}\sum_iw_iy_{ij}^2, \qquad B_{F,jk} = (1-\alpha_F)B^{\mathrm{rec}}_{F,jk} + \alpha_F\bar{\tilde\beta}_k\sum_iw_iy_{ij}(z_i - \bar\eta_{i,-k}), \tag{20}\] with \(x_{F,jk} = B_{F,jk}/A_{F,jk}\) and \(s_{F,jk} = A_{F,jk}^{-1/2}\). Compared with Equation 19, this branch omits the normalizer \(d_k\) and the coupling term, and it updates all features of factor \(k\) simultaneously. With \(\alpha_F = 0.5\) the pseudo-observation equals that of the unit-weight sum of the reconstruction terms and this branch, with half its precision; this is a statement about the same approximate kernel, not an exact posterior of the normalized joint target. In the evaluated fit \(\alpha_F = 0\), so Equation 20 reduces to Equation 18: the loading update is the reconstruction update of empirical-Bayes matrix factorization, with the point-exponential prior fitted over the \(p\) pseudo-observations of each factor.

A.8 Precision update

Write \(\mu_{ij} = \sum_kL_{ik}F_{jk}\). Under \(q\) the factors are independent, so \(E\mu_{ij} = \sum_k\bar L_{ik}\bar F_{jk}\) and \[ E\mu_{ij}^2 = \Big(\sum_k\bar L_{ik}\bar F_{jk}\Big)^2 + \sum_k\big(\overline{L_{ik}^2}\,\overline{F_{jk}^2} - \bar L_{ik}^2\bar F_{jk}^2\big), \] because \(\mathrm{Var}(\mu_{ij}) = \sum_k\mathrm{Var}(L_{ik}F_{jk})\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(L_{ik}F_{jk}) = \overline{L_{ik}^2}\,\overline{F_{jk}^2} - \bar L_{ik}^2\bar F_{jk}^2\). Hence \[ Q_j = \sum_iE_q(y_{ij} - \mu_{ij})^2 = \sum_i\Big[(y_{ij} - E\mu_{ij})^2 + \sum_k\big(\overline{L_{ik}^2}\,\overline{F_{jk}^2} - \bar L_{ik}^2\bar F_{jk}^2\big)\Big]. \] The expected log-likelihood in \(\tau_j\) is \(\frac n2\log\tau_j - \frac{\tau_j}{2}Q_j + c\); setting its derivative \(n/(2\tau_j) - Q_j/2\) to zero gives \[ \hat\tau_j = n/Q_j . \tag{21}\] The implementation floors \(Q_j\) at \(n \times 10^{-8}\), so \(\hat\tau_j \le 10^8\). There is no prior on \(\tau_j\).

A.9 Monitoring statistic and stopping rule

After each sweep the implementation computes \[ J = (1-\alpha)\,G + \alpha\,p\,S + \sum_k\big(\kappa_{L,k} + \kappa_{F,k} + \kappa_{\beta,k}\big), \tag{22}\] where \(G = \sum_j\big[\frac n2\log\tau_j - \frac{\tau_j}{2}Q_j\big]\) is the reconstruction log-likelihood without its constant, \(S = \ell_C(\hat\eta) - \frac12\sum_iw_i\mathrm{Var}_q(\eta_i)\) with \(\mathrm{Var}_q(\eta_i) = \sum_k\tilde Z_{ik}^2\mathrm{Var}_q(\tilde\beta_k)\) evaluated at the sweep’s starting predictor \(\hat\eta\), and each \(\kappa\) is a negative KL term computed from Equation 13. The algorithm stops at the first sweep after the fifth with \(|J_r - J_{r-1}|/|J_{r-1}| < 10^{-5}\).

\(J\) differs from the target Equation 9 in four ways. Its reconstruction and survival components are weighted by \(1-\alpha\) and \(\alpha p\). Its survival term uses \(\ell_C(\hat\eta)\) at the start of the sweep, whereas the expected working quadratic at the updated means would also include \(\sum_iu_i(\bar\eta_i - \hat\eta_i) - \frac12\sum_iw_i(\bar\eta_i - \hat\eta_i)^2\). Its survival term uses the working curvature of A.2. And for the activities, whose \(n\) pseudo-observations share one precision \(A_{L,k}\), the implemented \(\kappa_{L,k}\) includes the Gaussian log-normalizer \(\frac12\log(A_{L,k}/2\pi)\) once rather than \(n\) times as in Equation 14, so \[ \kappa_{L,k}^{\mathrm{impl}} = \kappa_{L,k} + \frac{n-1}{2}\log\frac{A_{L,k}}{2\pi}, \] a discrepancy that changes with \(A_{L,k}\) across sweeps. These features affect only the stopping rule, not the coordinate updates. \(J\) is therefore a convergence monitor, not an evidence lower bound, and the updates are not guaranteed to increase it.

A.10 Orientation and prediction

After the loop, the implementation compares the training concordance of \(\eta\) with 0.5 once and negates \(\bar{\tilde\beta}\) if \(\eta\) is discordant with risk. For the evaluated fit this check left \(\eta\) concordant with longer survival, so the risk score is \(-\eta\) for every held-out cohort, a direction fixed before validation. The stored second moments of \(\tilde\beta\) for this fit equal the squared means, so its posterior variances are zero and no coefficient uncertainty can be reported.

For a new patient with data standardized within its own cohort, prediction restricts \(\bar F\) to the training features \(\mathcal G\) measured in that cohort and keeps the stored norms \(D_*\), formed from \(\bar F\) at the start of the final sweep: \[ \eta_{\mathrm{new}} = y_{\mathrm{new},\mathcal G}^\top\bar F_{\mathcal G}D_*^{-1}\bar{\tilde\beta}. \] \(D_*\) differs slightly from the norms of the final \(\bar F\) (by less than \(2\times10^{-3}\) in absolute value for each retained program in the evaluated fit), and the stored norms include a ridge, \(d_k = (\lVert\bar F_{\cdot k}\rVert_2^2 + 10^{-10})^{1/2}\), so a zero column gives a zero projection.

A.11 Joint target and evaluated algorithm

Appendix B. Multimodal derivations

This appendix derives the updates of the evaluated multimodal framework from its likelihood, priors and variational family, ending each coordinate update at the normal-means inputs \(x = B/A\) and \(s = A^{-1/2}\). It uses the notation and the general results of Appendix A: the reduction to normal means and the KL identity (A.3), point-exponential posteriors (A.4), and the normal coefficient prior (A.5).

B.1 Model and target

For modalities \(m \in \{\mathrm{expr}, \mathrm{meth}\}\), patients \(i\), features \(j\) and factors \(k\), \[ y_{mij} = \mu_{mj} + \sum_k l_{ik}f_{mjk} + e_{mij}, \qquad e_{mij} \sim N(0, \tau_{mj}^{-1}), \tag{23}\] so that \[ \ell_Y = \sum_{m,i,j}\Big\{\tfrac12\log\frac{\tau_{mj}}{2\pi} - \frac{\tau_{mj}}{2}\Big(y_{mij} - \mu_{mj} - \sum_kl_{ik}f_{mjk}\Big)^2\Big\}. \tag{24}\] The priors are \[ l_{ik} \sim g_{L,k} = (1-\pi_{L,k})\delta_0 + \pi_{L,k}\,\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_{L,k}), \qquad f_{mjk} \sim g_{mk} = (1-\pi_{mk})\delta_0 + \pi_{mk}\,\mathrm{Laplace}(0, \lambda_{mk}^{-1}), \tag{25}\] and \(\beta_k \sim N(0, \sigma_k^2)\). Survival enters through the Breslow partial log-likelihood \(\ell_C(\eta)\) of Equation 8 with \[ \eta_i = \sum_kZ_{ik}\beta_k, \qquad Z_{ik} = \sum_{m,j}\tilde y_{mij}f_{mjk}, \qquad \tilde y_{mij} = y_{mij} - \mu_{mj}. \tag{26}\] The intercepts \(\mu_{mj}\), precisions \(\tau_{mj}\) and prior parameters are point estimates. With the mean-field family \(q = \prod_{i,k}q(l_{ik})\prod_{m,j,k}q(f_{mjk})\prod_kq(\beta_k)\), the target is \[ \mathcal L(q) = E_q\ell_Y + E_q\ell_C(\eta) - \sum_{i,k}\mathrm{KL}(q(l_{ik})\Vert g_{L,k}) - \sum_{m,j,k}\mathrm{KL}(q(f_{mjk})\Vert g_{mk}) - \sum_k\mathrm{KL}(q(\beta_k)\Vert N(0,\sigma_k^2)). \] Unlike the single-modality algorithm, the multimodal algorithm treats \(F_m\) as random inside the projection, so the coefficient and loading updates carry projection uncertainty.

B.2 Working approximation

The coordinate updates replace \(E_q\ell_C\) by the expectation of the working quadratic Equation 10 at the predictor \(\hat\eta = \bar\eta\) from the start of the outer sweep, written without dividing by \(w_i\): \[ \ell_C(\eta) \approx c + \sum_i\big(h_i\eta_i - \tfrac12w_i\eta_i^2\big), \qquad h_i = u_i + w_i\bar\eta_i, \quad w_i = a_i, \tag{27}\] with \(u_i\) and \(a_i\) as in A.2. There is no floor on \(w_i\). The quantities \((w, h)\) are held fixed for the inner sweeps of an outer sweep. The expected surrogate is \[ \sum_i\Big[h_iE_q\eta_i - \tfrac12w_iE_q\eta_i^2\Big]. \]

B.3 Intercept

Only \(\ell_Y\) is used to update \(\mu_{mj}\). Its derivative is \[ \frac{\partial E_q\ell_Y}{\partial\mu_{mj}} = \tau_{mj}\sum_i\Big(y_{mij} - \mu_{mj} - \sum_k\bar l_{ik}\bar f_{mjk}\Big), \] and setting it to zero gives \[ \hat\mu_{mj} = \frac1n\sum_i\Big(y_{mij} - \sum_k\bar l_{ik}\bar f_{mjk}\Big). \tag{28}\] The intercept is updated at the start of each outer sweep and for each candidate in the removal check, after which every block is re-centered, \(\tilde Y_m = Y_m - \mathbf 1\hat\mu_m^\top\), and the projection moments are recomputed from the centered data. With fixed loadings, replacing \(\tilde y\) by \(y\) in Equation 26 shifts every \(\eta_i\) by the same constant \(\sum_{m,j,k}\mu_{mj}f_{mjk}\beta_k\), which leaves the exact partial likelihood and the concordance index unchanged. Under \(q\), however, this shift is random, and the expected working surrogate need not be invariant to it. Updating the intercept from the reconstruction alone is therefore an implementation choice, not a consequence of shift invariance.

B.4 Projection and predictor moments

Under \(q\) the loadings of different features are independent, so \[ \bar Z_{ik} = \sum_{m,j}\tilde y_{mij}\bar f_{mjk}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik}) = \sum_{m,j}\tilde y_{mij}^2\,\mathrm{Var}(f_{mjk}), \qquad E(Z_{ik}^2) = \bar Z_{ik}^2 + \mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik}). \tag{29}\] Factors are independent of each other and \(\beta\) is independent of \(F\), so \(\bar\eta_i = \sum_k\bar Z_{ik}\bar\beta_k\) and \[ \mathrm{Var}(\eta_i) = \sum_k\mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik}\beta_k) = \sum_k\big\{E(Z_{ik}^2)\overline{\beta_k^2} - \bar Z_{ik}^2\bar\beta_k^2\big\} = \sum_k\big\{\overline{\beta_k^2}\,\mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik}) + \bar Z_{ik}^2\,\mathrm{Var}(\beta_k)\big\}. \tag{30}\] The two forms agree because \((\bar Z^2 + V_Z)(\bar\beta^2 + V_\beta) - \bar Z^2\bar\beta^2 = (\bar\beta^2 + V_\beta)V_Z + \bar Z^2V_\beta\). Predictors of different patients share the random loadings and coefficients and are therefore correlated; only their marginal moments are used below.

B.5 Shared activities

\(\eta\) does not depend on \(L\), so only \(\ell_Y\) contributes. Define the random residual \(r_{mij}^{(-k)} = \tilde y_{mij} - \sum_{l\ne k}l_{il}f_{mjl}\) with mean \(R_{mij}^{(-k)} = \tilde y_{mij} - \sum_{l\ne k}\bar l_{il}\bar f_{mjl}\). As in A.6, \[ E_{-l_{ik}}(r_{mij}^{(-k)} - l_{ik}f_{mjk})^2 = c_{mij} - 2l_{ik}R_{mij}^{(-k)}\bar f_{mjk} + l_{ik}^2\overline{f_{mjk}^2}. \] Multiplying by \(-\tau_{mj}/2\) and summing over both modalities and all features, \[ A_{L,k} = \sum_{m,j}\tau_{mj}\overline{f_{mjk}^2}, \qquad B_{L,ik} = \sum_{m,j}\tau_{mj}R_{mij}^{(-k)}\bar f_{mjk}, \qquad x_{L,ik} = B_{L,ik}/A_{L,k}, \qquad s_{L,k} = A_{L,k}^{-1/2}. \tag{31}\] Each \(q(l_{ik})\) is the point-exponential posterior of A.4 under the current \(g_{L,k}\). After the column is updated, \((\pi_{L,k}, \lambda_{L,k})\) is re-estimated by maximizing the marginal likelihood of the \(n\) pseudo-observations (A.3), which can return \(\pi_{L,k} = 0\) and so remove the column.

B.6 Modality-specific loadings

Reconstruction terms. As in A.7, within modality \(m\), \[ A^{\mathrm{rec}}_{mjk} = \tau_{mj}\sum_i\overline{l_{ik}^2}, \qquad B^{\mathrm{rec}}_{mjk} = \tau_{mj}\sum_i\bar l_{ik}R_{mij}^{(-k)}. \]

Survival terms. Fix \((m, j, k)\) and write \(f = f_{mjk}\), \(a_i = \tilde y_{mij}\), \(U_i = Z_{ik} - a_if\) (the projection excluding feature \(j\) of modality \(m\)) and \(V_i = \eta_{i,-k} = \sum_{l\ne k}Z_{il}\beta_l\). Then \[ \eta_i = \beta_k(a_if + U_i) + V_i, \qquad \eta_i^2 = a_i^2f^2\beta_k^2 + 2a_if\big(\beta_k^2U_i + \beta_kV_i\big) + (\beta_kU_i + V_i)^2 . \] Under \(q\), \(f\), \(\beta_k\), \(U_i\) and \(V_i\) are mutually independent, so \(E(\beta_k^2U_i) = \overline{\beta_k^2}\,\bar U_i\) and \(E(\beta_kV_i) = \bar\beta_k\bar V_i\). Substituting into \(h_i\eta_i - \frac12w_i\eta_i^2\) and keeping the terms in \(f\), \[ f\,a_i\Big[\bar\beta_k\big(h_i - w_i\bar V_i\big) - w_i\overline{\beta_k^2}\,\bar U_i\Big] - \tfrac12f^2\,w_ia_i^2\,\overline{\beta_k^2}. \] The quadratic coefficient uses \(\overline{\beta_k^2}\) because \(\beta_k\) multiplies \(f\) inside a square.

Combined update. Adding the reconstruction terms and summing over patients, \[ A_{mjk} = \tau_{mj}\sum_i\overline{l_{ik}^2} + \overline{\beta_k^2}\sum_iw_i\tilde y_{mij}^2, \tag{32}\] \[ B_{mjk} = \tau_{mj}\sum_i\bar l_{ik}R^{(-k)}_{mij} + \bar\beta_k\sum_i\tilde y_{mij}\big(h_i - w_i\bar V_i\big) - \overline{\beta_k^2}\sum_iw_i\tilde y_{mij}\bar U_i , \tag{33}\] with \(x_{mjk} = B_{mjk}/A_{mjk}\) and \(s_{mjk} = A_{mjk}^{-1/2}\). The last term of Equation 33 couples feature \(j\) to every other feature of factor \(k\) through \(\bar U_i\): the survival information a feature receives depends on how much of the projection the other features already supply. Features are therefore updated one at a time (Gauss–Seidel), and after each update the projection moments are refreshed by the change in that feature’s moments, \(\bar Z_{ik} \leftarrow \bar Z_{ik} + \tilde y_{mij}(\bar f^{\mathrm{new}} - \bar f^{\mathrm{old}})\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik}) \leftarrow \mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik}) + \tilde y_{mij}^2\{\mathrm{Var}(f^{\mathrm{new}}) - \mathrm{Var}(f^{\mathrm{old}})\}\). Both survival terms vanish only when \(\bar\beta_k\) and \(\overline{\beta_k^2}\) are both small; a coefficient with near-zero mean but substantial variance still contributes through \(\overline{\beta_k^2}\), and a point mass at zero removes both.

Point-Laplace posterior. With prior \((1-\pi)\delta_0 + \pi\frac\lambda2e^{-\lambda|f|}\), the positive half-line is handled exactly as the point-exponential slab of A.4 with \(\lambda\) replaced by \(\lambda/2\) in the prefactor: with \(m_+ = x - \lambda s^2\), \[ \int_0^\infty N(x;\, f, s^2)\,\tfrac{\pi\lambda}{2}e^{-\lambda f}\,df = \tfrac{\pi\lambda}{2}\,e^{-\lambda x + \lambda^2s^2/2}\,\Phi(m_+/s). \] For the negative half-line substitute \(f = -f'\) with \(f' > 0\). Then \(N(x; -f', s^2) = N(-x; f', s^2)\), and completing the square as in A.4 with \(x\) replaced by \(-x\) gives, with \(m_- = -x - \lambda s^2\), \[ \int_{-\infty}^0 N(x;\, f, s^2)\,\tfrac{\pi\lambda}{2}e^{\lambda f}\,df = \tfrac{\pi\lambda}{2}\,e^{\lambda x + \lambda^2s^2/2}\,\Phi(m_-/s). \] Normalizing the three components gives the posterior weights \(\omega_0 \propto (1-\pi)N(x; 0, s^2)\), \(\omega_+\) and \(\omega_-\) proportional to the two integrals, and the marginal likelihood \(p_g(x)\) as their sum. The positive component is \(N(m_+, s^2)\) truncated to \((0, \infty)\) and the negative component is the negative of \(N(m_-, s^2)\) truncated to \((0, \infty)\). With \(M_+\) and \(S_+\) from Equation 15, \[ \bar f = \omega_+M_+(m_+) - \omega_-M_+(m_-), \qquad \overline{f^2} = \omega_+S_+(m_+) + \omega_-S_+(m_-). \tag{34}\] Tail evaluations of \(\log\Phi\) and \(\phi/\Phi\) use asymptotic expansions for numerical stability.

Prior refit and cached penalties. The point-Laplace parameters \((\pi_{mk}, \lambda_{mk})\) are held fixed while the features of modality \(m\) and factor \(k\) are updated, and are then re-estimated by maximizing the marginal likelihood of that sweep’s \(p_m\) pseudo-observations. The KL penalties stored for these coordinates are computed by Equation 13 against the prior used during the sweep, not the refitted prior. The same holds for the activities in B.5.

B.7 Survival coefficients

Write \(\eta_i = Z_{ik}\beta_k + V_i\). Expanding \((Z_{ik}\beta_k + V_i)^2 = Z_{ik}^2\beta_k^2 + 2Z_{ik}V_i\beta_k + V_i^2\) and using the independence of \(Z_{ik}\) and \(V_i\) under \(q\), the terms of the expected surrogate in \(\beta_k\) are \[ \beta_k\sum_i\bar Z_{ik}\big(h_i - w_i\bar V_i\big) - \tfrac12\beta_k^2\sum_iw_iE(Z_{ik}^2), \] so \[ A_{\beta,k} = \sum_iw_i\big\{\bar Z_{ik}^2 + \mathrm{Var}(Z_{ik})\big\}, \qquad B_{\beta,k} = \sum_i\bar Z_{ik}\big(h_i - w_i\bar V_i\big), \qquad x_{\beta,k} = B_{\beta,k}/A_{\beta,k}, \qquad s_{\beta,k} = A_{\beta,k}^{-1/2}. \tag{35}\] Unlike Equation 16, \(A_{\beta,k}\) includes the projection variance, so loading uncertainty shrinks the coefficient, and there is no weight \(\alpha\). As in A.5, the prior variance is \(\hat\sigma_k^2 = \max(0, x_{\beta,k}^2 - s_{\beta,k}^2)\); if it is zero, \(q(\beta_k) = \delta_0\) and the KL term is zero. Otherwise \[ \mathrm{Var}(\beta_k) = \big(A_{\beta,k} + \hat\sigma_k^{-2}\big)^{-1}, \qquad \bar\beta_k = \mathrm{Var}(\beta_k)\,B_{\beta,k}, \] which equals the posterior mean \(x\hat\sigma^2/(\hat\sigma^2 + s^2)\) of A.5. For \(q = N(\bar\beta, v)\) and \(g = N(0, \sigma^2)\), taking the expectation of \(\log q - \log g = -\frac12\log(v/\sigma^2) - (\beta - \bar\beta)^2/(2v) + \beta^2/(2\sigma^2)\) under \(q\) gives \[ \mathrm{KL}(q\,\Vert\,g) = \tfrac12\Big[\frac{v + \bar\beta^2}{\sigma^2} - 1 - \log\frac{v}{\sigma^2}\Big]. \] A factor is classified survival-active when \(|\bar\beta_k|/\mathrm{sd}(\beta_k) \ge 1.96\), an operational rule on the posterior mean and standard deviation, not an adjusted test. The coefficients are initialized from a Cox fit on standardized initial projections, transformed back to the projection scale.

B.8 Precisions

Summing the expected squared residual of A.8 over patients within each modality and feature, \[ Q_{mj} = \sum_i\Big[\Big(\tilde y_{mij} - \sum_k\bar l_{ik}\bar f_{mjk}\Big)^2 + \sum_k\big(\overline{l_{ik}^2}\,\overline{f_{mjk}^2} - \bar l_{ik}^2\bar f_{mjk}^2\big)\Big], \] and maximizing \(\frac n2\log\tau_{mj} - \frac{\tau_{mj}}{2}Q_{mj}\) gives \[ \hat\tau_{mj} = n/Q_{mj}. \tag{36}\] These are unregularized maximum-likelihood values. If \(Q_{mj} = 0\) the maximum likelihood estimate does not exist; the implementation stops with an error rather than imposing a floor. One precision per modality and a Gamma prior on \(\tau_{mj}\) are implemented alternatives that were not used.

B.9 Scale canonicalization

For \(c_k > 0\) consider the map \((l_{\cdot k}, f_{mk}, \beta_k) \mapsto (c_kl_{\cdot k}, f_{mk}/c_k, c_k\beta_k)\).
