Substituting, \((c_kl_{ik})(f_{mjk}/c_k) = l_{ik}f_{mjk}\), so each \(LF_m^\top\) is unchanged; \(Z_{ik} \mapsto Z_{ik}/c_k\), so \(Z_{ik}\beta_k \mapsto (Z_{ik}/c_k)(c_k\beta_k) = Z_{ik}\beta_k\) and \(\eta\) is unchanged. The likelihood therefore does not determine the scale of a factor, and coordinate updates can drift along this direction. After each factor’s coefficient update the implementation sets \(c_k = \mathrm{sd}(\bar Z_{\cdot k})\) over training patients and applies the map to the variational distributions, which transforms their moments as \[ \bar l_{\cdot k} \mapsto c_k\bar l_{\cdot k}, \quad \overline{l^2_{\cdot k}} \mapsto c_k^2\overline{l^2_{\cdot k}}, \quad \bar f_{mk} \mapsto \bar f_{mk}/c_k, \quad \overline{f^2_{mk}} \mapsto \overline{f^2_{mk}}/c_k^2, \quad \bar\beta_k \mapsto c_k\bar\beta_k, \quad \overline{\beta_k^2} \mapsto c_k^2\overline{\beta_k^2}, \] and hence \(\bar Z_{\cdot k} \mapsto \bar Z_{\cdot k}/c_k\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Z_{\cdot k}) \mapsto \mathrm{Var}(Z_{\cdot k})/c_k^2\).

The priors are transformed by the same map, so that each transformed prior is the distribution of the transformed coordinate (its pushforward). If \(l \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)\) then \(c\,l \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda/c)\); if \(f \sim \mathrm{Laplace}(0, \lambda^{-1})\) then \(f/c \sim \mathrm{Laplace}(0, (c\lambda)^{-1})\); and if \(\beta \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) then \(c\beta \sim N(0, c^2\sigma^2)\). The point-mass weights are unchanged. Hence \[ \lambda_{L,k} \mapsto \lambda_{L,k}/c_k, \qquad \lambda_{mk} \mapsto c_k\lambda_{mk}, \qquad \sigma_k^2 \mapsto c_k^2\sigma_k^2 . \tag{37}\] Prior density values themselves change by the Jacobian \(1/c_k\) or \(c_k\); what is preserved is the probability of each transformed event. Because the posterior and the prior are transformed by the same bijection, each KL divergence is unchanged. After the map, \(\mathrm{sd}(\bar Z_{\cdot k}) = 1\) in training, so a coefficient is per training SD of the mean joint projection. When \(\mathrm{sd}(\bar Z_{\cdot k})\) is numerically zero, the implementation uses \(c_k = 1\), and that column does not acquire SD one. Canonicalization changes neither the fitted reconstruction nor the predictor, but it is applied between coordinate updates and therefore changes the path of the algorithm.

B.10 Stopping rule

For a fitted quantity \(X\) (each \(\bar L\bar F_m^\top\), and \(\bar\eta\)), the relative change between consecutive outer sweeps is \[ \frac{\max|X_{\mathrm{new}} - X_{\mathrm{old}}|}{\max\big(1,\ \max|X_{\mathrm{old}}|,\ \max|X_{\mathrm{new}}|\big)}, \] and the algorithm stops when every such change is below \(10^{-4}\), or after 500 outer sweeps. These quantities are invariant to the map of B.9, which is why they are used instead of changes in posterior moments.

B.11 Removal score and factor removal

When the coordinate loop ends, by meeting the criterion or by reaching the cap, the removal check computes for each factor \(k\) \[ \Delta_k = \mathcal S\big(\text{factors} \ne k\big) - \mathcal S\big(\text{all factors}\big), \tag{38}\] where \(\mathcal S\) is Equation 6 evaluated with factor \(k\)’s activities, loadings and coefficient set to zero and its KL terms removed, the other factors’ posteriors held fixed, and \(\mu\) and \(\tau\) re-estimated. The KL terms of \(\mathcal S\) are the cached penalties of B.5 and B.6, computed against the priors in force at each coordinate’s latest update. If \(\max_k\Delta_k \ge 0\), the factor with the largest \(\Delta_k\) is deleted, the algorithm restarts from the remaining factors’ moments and priors with \(K - 1\) factors, and the check repeats after that fit. A deletion therefore improves the implemented removal score before the remaining factors adapt. It is not guaranteed to improve the exact marginal likelihood or an ELBO evaluated at the current posterior and current priors.

The survival component of \(\mathcal S\) is \(\ell_C(\bar\eta)\), whereas the target uses \(E_q\ell_C(\eta)\). Because \(\ell_C\) is concave in \(\eta\), Jensen’s inequality gives \(E_q\ell_C(\eta) \le \ell_C(\bar\eta)\), so the plug-in term is an upper approximation to its posterior expectation. Jensen’s inequality does not imply that the gap grows with every marginal variance: adding the same random shift to every \(\eta_i\) increases each \(\mathrm{Var}(\eta_i)\) but leaves \(\ell_C\), and hence the gap, unchanged. A second-order expansion gives \(E_q\ell_C(\eta) \approx \ell_C(\bar\eta) - \frac12\mathrm{tr}\{\mathcal H\,\mathrm{Cov}_q(\eta)\}\), with \(\mathcal H\) the exact negative Hessian of A.2 and \(\mathrm{Cov}_q(\eta)\) the full patient-by-patient covariance. The variance-penalized alternative used in the simulation, \(\ell_C(\bar\eta) - \frac12\sum_iw_i\mathrm{Var}(\eta_i)\), replaces \(\mathcal H\) by the diagonal working curvature and ignores the covariances. Neither form makes \(\mathcal S\) a lower bound on the marginal likelihood, and the coordinate updates are not guaranteed to increase it. On real data the reconstruction component, which sums over every feature of both modalities, dominates \(\mathcal S\).

B.12 Prediction

For a new patient with features aligned to the training features, \(\eta_{\mathrm{new}} = \sum_my_{m,\mathrm{new}}^\top\bar F_m\bar\beta\), using data that are not centered. With fixed posterior means, centering at the training intercept would shift every score by the constant \(\sum_m\hat\mu_m^\top\bar F_m\bar\beta\), which changes neither the ranking of patients nor the concordance index. Higher \(\eta\) denotes higher risk, a direction fixed before validation.
